title: The Explorers
sub: Ten explorers, two from each country. Which country they sailed for, where they went, and what the book says they are famous for.
cite: CKHG Grade 5, Unit 3: The Age of Exploration, Student Reader
note: Every question and every hint comes from this reader and nothing else. The page number beside a hint is the printed page in the Student Reader.

explorers.name: Bartolomeu Dias
explorers.fact: 1487, three ships. First European round the southern tip of Africa and into the Indian Ocean. Named it the Cape of Storms — today the Cape of Good Hope.

explorers.name: Vasco da Gama
explorers.fact: 1497, four ships from Lisbon. Round the Cape and up the east coast of Africa. A pilot from Malindi and the trade winds took him across the Indian Ocean in twenty-three days to Calicut in India.

explorers.name: Christopher Columbus
explorers.fact: Italian, turned down by Portugal and France. Ferdinand and Isabella paid. Sailed west in 1492 with the Niña, the Pinta and the Santa Maria, and landed in the Bahamas on an island he named San Salvador.

explorers.name: Ferdinand Magellan
explorers.fact: Born in Portugal, sailed for Spain. 1519, five ships and 277 men. Found the strait at the tip of South America and named the Pacific Ocean. Killed in the Philippines.

explorers.name: John Cabot
explorers.fact: Giovanni Caboto, a Venetian spice trader. Backed by Henry VII and the merchants of Bristol. 1497, one ship and a crew of eighteen, to “new found land,” hunting the Northwest Passage.

explorers.name: Sir Francis Drake
explorers.fact: A pirate for Queen Elizabeth, robbing Spanish ships. Set out in 1577 with five ships and followed Magellan’s example round the world, ending with one ship, the Golden Hind.

explorers.name: Jacques Cartier
explorers.fact: 1534, sent by France’s king. Newfoundland, Labrador and the Gulf of St. Lawrence, then up the St. Lawrence River. Named the hill Mount Royal, now part of Montreal.

explorers.name: Samuel de Champlain
explorers.fact: The key figure in settling New France. 1603 to Maine and Nova Scotia; in 1608 he moved the settlement to the site of Quebec City on the St. Lawrence.

explorers.name: Henry Hudson
explorers.fact: An English explorer hired by the Dutch East India Company in 1609. Sailed the Half Moon and claimed land at the mouth of what is now the Hudson River for the Netherlands.

explorers.name: Abel Tasman
explorers.fact: Dutch. In 1643 he landed on the island now named Tasmania, and by sailing around Australia proved it was a huge island unconnected to any other land.

quizzes.name: Quiz 1
quizzes.title: Multiple choice
quizzes.how: Two questions on each explorer: which country he sailed for, and what the book says he did.

items.q: Which country did Bartolomeu Dias sail for?
items.hint: He set out in 1487 with a fleet of three ships, pushing farther down the west coast of Africa than any European had gone before.
items.why: Portugal. He was one of Prince Henry’s country’s captains, working his way down the African coast.

items.q: What was Bartolomeu Dias the first European to do?
opts: Sail around the southern tip of Africa into the Indian Ocean
Sail all the way around the world and return home to Portugal
items.hint: His fleet was blown offshore in a storm. When land came back into sight it was on the wrong side of the ship — the west, not the east.
items.why: He had rounded Africa without knowing it. The book says he “was the first European to find a route to the Indian Ocean.”

items.q: Which country did Vasco da Gama sail for?
items.hint: He led a fleet of four ships out of Lisbon in 1497, following the route Dias had opened.
items.why: Portugal. Lisbon is its capital, and da Gama carried on where Dias stopped.

items.q: Which Indian city did Vasco da Gama’s fleet reach after crossing the Indian Ocean?
items.hint: A friendly welcome at Malindi got him a ship’s pilot, and the trade winds did the rest — twenty-three days across the open ocean.
items.why: Calicut, a major trading city on the southwest coast of India, known today as Kozhikode. Mombasa, Malindi and Mozambique were the African ports along the way.

items.q: Christopher Columbus was Italian. Which country paid for his voyage of 1492?
items.hint: He spent seven years asking. Portugal said no and France kept putting him off, until a king and queen finally agreed.
items.why: Spain. King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella paid, and told him to claim any new lands for them.

items.q: Where did Columbus actually make landfall on 12 October 1492?
items.hint: He was certain he had reached Asia, and he named the island San Salvador. The people there were the Taino.
items.why: The Bahamas — islands just east of what is now Florida. He thought it was the East Indies, which is why he called the people “Indians.”

items.q: Ferdinand Magellan was born in Portugal. Which country did he sail for?
items.hint: His temper cost him the support of the Portuguese crown, so in 1517 a friend persuaded him to ask somebody else.
items.why: Spain. When he was given command of a Spanish expedition he “turned his back on Portugal forever.”

items.q: Why did Magellan give the Pacific Ocean its name?
opts: Because it was the largest ocean he had ever crossed
Because its waters were so peaceful
Because he made peace with his crew there
Because the king of Spain asked him to
items.hint: He had just fought his way through a month of cliffs and violent tides in the strait. What came next was a shock.
items.why: The fleet came out of the strait into a vast, calm sea. “Because the waters were so pleasantly peaceful, he named the body of water the Pacific Ocean.”

items.q: John Cabot was a Venetian spice trader. Which country did he sail for?
items.hint: Spain and Portugal both turned his plan down, so he moved his family to Bristol and changed his name.
items.why: England. Giovanni Caboto became John Cabot, and King Henry VII and the Bristol merchants backed him.

items.q: Cabot’s crew came home with no spices and no silks. What did they describe that made the voyage count as a success?
opts: A short sea passage running through North America all the way to Asia
Waters so full of fish they could scoop them out in baskets
Gold and silver taken from a Spanish treasure ship
A strait at the southern tip of South America
items.hint: They had crossed the North Atlantic in five weeks and reached somewhere they called “new found land.” Think about what those waters are famous for.
items.why: The fishing. “The voyage was judged a success, and another trip was planned for the following year.”

items.q: Which country did Sir Francis Drake sail for?
items.hint: He robbed Spanish and Portuguese ships and handed the treasure to his queen, Elizabeth.
items.why: England. To the Spanish he was a pirate; at home he was one of the greatest sea captains in history.

items.q: What was the name of the one ship Drake still had when he reached the west coast of South America?
items.hint: He had set out in 1577 with five ships and 164 men. By then he was down to fifty-eight men and a single ship.
items.why: The Golden Hind — the ship he sailed round the world, following Magellan’s example through the Straits of Magellan.

items.q: Which country did Jacques Cartier sail for?
items.hint: In 1534 a king asked him to explore the coast of North America, and he claimed the land around the Gulf of St. Lawrence for that king.
items.why: France. The book calls him “a French sea captain.”

items.q: What did Cartier name the hill that is now part of the city of Montreal?
items.hint: He had sailed up the St. Lawrence River and stopped at a Native American village on an island.
items.why: Mount Royal. “This site eventually became part of the Canadian city of Montreal.”

items.q: Which country did Samuel de Champlain sail for?
items.hint: He was the key figure in settling the land his country called New France, built on the fur trade.
items.why: France. New France grew around his settlement on the St. Lawrence.

items.q: What did Champlain do in 1608?
opts: He sailed up the Mississippi to the Gulf of Mexico
He moved his settlement to the site of Quebec City
He found a Northwest Passage to Asia
items.hint: He first sailed to New France in 1603 and put his first settlement in Nova Scotia. Five years later he moved it somewhere better.
items.why: He moved it to the site of Quebec City, on the banks of the St. Lawrence, and built a town on the heights above the river.

items.q: Henry Hudson was English. Which country did he explore for in 1609?
items.hint: He was hired by a trading company that already had a monopoly on the spice route east of the Cape of Good Hope.
items.why: The Netherlands. The Dutch East India Company hired him, and he claimed the land at the mouth of the Hudson River for them.

items.q: What was the name of the small ship Hudson sailed in 1609?
items.hint: He took a small crew and headed north along the coast of Norway first, before changing his mind and turning west.
items.why: The Half Moon. The Discovery was the English ship he sailed the next year, the one his crew mutinied on.

items.q: Which country did Abel Tasman sail for?
items.hint: He was one of many explorers from his country who set out across the Pacific from their trading centre at Java.
items.why: The Netherlands. He is in the chapter on Dutch trade, alongside Dirk Hartog.

items.q: What did Abel Tasman prove by sailing around Australia?
opts: That it was joined to the southern tip of South America
That it was a huge island, not joined to any other land
That it was part of the Spice Islands
items.hint: In 1643 he landed on an island off Australia’s southeastern coast that is named after him.
items.why: That Australia “was a huge island unconnected to any other land.” The island he landed on is Tasmania.

quizzes.name: Quiz 2
quizzes.title: Who said it?
quizzes.how: Each one is an explorer talking about himself. Pick his name. A name can be the answer more than once.

items.q: “I was the first European to sail around the southern tip of Africa.”
items.hint: A storm blew his fleet offshore, and he only realised what had happened when land reappeared on the west side of the ship.
items.why: Dias, in 1487. He had rounded Africa without knowing it.

items.q: “I called it the Cape of Storms. Today you call it the Cape of Good Hope.”
items.hint: He spotted it as he turned his fleet around and headed north for home.
items.why: Dias named it Cabo Tormentoso, the Cape of Storms.

items.q: “A pilot from Malindi and the trade winds carried us to Calicut in twenty-three days.”
items.hint: At Mombasa and Mozambique the Arab traders tried to seize his ships. Malindi was the port where the welcome was friendly.
items.why: Da Gama, 1497–99, the first to take the sea route all the way to India.

items.q: “I kept a secret log so my crew would not know how far we had really sailed.”
items.hint: If they covered thirty-nine leagues he would tell them thirty. He did not want them frightened by the distance.
items.why: Columbus. His crew threatened mutiny anyway.

items.q: “I called the people I met Indians, because I was certain I had reached the East Indies.”
items.hint: He was actually in the Bahamas, and the people were the Taino.
items.why: Columbus. “The name stuck,” says the book, even after later explorers proved him wrong.

items.q: “The water was so peaceful after that terrible strait that I named the ocean for it.”
items.hint: It had taken his fleet more than a month to get through, between tall cliffs and violent tides.
items.why: Magellan named the Pacific Ocean.

items.q: “I was killed in the Philippines, and my crew sailed home without me.”
items.hint: Juan Sebastián del Cano took command and brought one ship and eighteen men back to Spain in 1522.
items.why: Magellan. He never completed the voyage round the world that is named after him.

items.q: “King Henry VII and the merchants of Bristol paid for my voyage.”
items.hint: He was Venetian, and both Spain and Portugal had already turned him down.
items.why: John Cabot — Giovanni Caboto before he moved to England.

items.q: “We brought home no spices, but we told them of waters so full of fish you could scoop them out in baskets.”
items.hint: He had crossed the North Atlantic with one ship and a crew of eighteen and reached “new found land.”
items.why: Cabot. It was enough for the voyage to be judged a success.

items.q: “I robbed Spanish ships and gave the treasure to my queen.”
items.hint: The Spanish ambassador called him “the master-thief of the unknown world.”
items.why: Drake, working for Queen Elizabeth I.

items.q: “I followed Magellan’s example and sailed around the world in the Golden Hind.”
items.hint: He set out in 1577 with five ships, and went through the Straits of Magellan.
items.why: Drake. He was the second to sail around the world, after Magellan’s crew.

items.q: “Native Americans taught my men to brew a drink from evergreen trees, and it cured their scurvy.”
items.hint: The snow was four feet deep, and many of his men had already died of cold and sickness.
items.why: Cartier. The book notes that such a brew is rich in vitamin C.

items.q: “I founded a settlement on the St. Lawrence that became Quebec City.”
items.hint: He built it on the heights, at a point where the river narrows.
items.why: Champlain, in 1608, after starting in Nova Scotia in 1603.

items.q: “I was English, but the Dutch East India Company hired me to find the Northwest Passage.”
items.hint: He sailed the Half Moon, and a river, a bay and a strait are all named after him.
items.why: Hudson. English by birth, exploring for the Netherlands.

items.q: “By sailing all the way around it, I proved Australia was one huge island.”
items.hint: In 1643 he landed on an island off Australia’s southeastern coast that now carries his name.
items.why: Tasman. The island is Tasmania.
